title: Analysis: 84% of nations miss deadline to identify ‘nature-harming’ subsidies by 2025  - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief's analysis of 134 national reports finds only 21 countries (16%) fully identified their biodiversity-harming subsidies by the 2025 Global Biodiversity Framework deadline, with the 32 disclosing countries reporting nearly $270bn/year in such subsidies — a figure experts call just the 'tip of the iceberg' against global estimates of $1.7-3.2tn.

insights.claim: Only 21 of 134 countries that submitted national reports to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) by 1 July 2026 say they have fully identified their biodiversity-harming subsidies, meaning roughly 84% missed the 2025 disclosure deadline under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A near-universal miss on a headline 2025 biodiversity milestone signals weak enforcement momentum heading into COP17, useful for gauging policy risk/reward on subsidy-exposed sectors.
insights.locator: Just 21 countries appear to have met the 2025 goal

insights.claim: The 32 countries that have identified some or all of their harmful subsidies collectively report spending an estimated $269.86bn annually on biodiversity-harming subsidies and incentives, based on Carbon Brief's tally of national report figures converted to US dollars and inflation-adjusted to 2025.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gives a disclosed fiscal baseline against which future subsidy-reform pledges (and the $500bn 2030 phase-out target) can be tracked.
insights.locator: The 32 countries that have identified some or all subsidies spend almost $270bn

insights.claim: Business for Nature CEO Eva Zabey says the disclosed $270bn figure is 'just the tip of the iceberg,' pointing to a 2022 estimate from the non-profit B Team that puts the true global scale of nature-harming subsidies as high as $1.8tn — meaning disclosed data may capture only about 15% of actual global exposure.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Suggests the true fiscal/biodiversity liability tied to harmful subsidies is far larger than official disclosures imply — a gap investors and policymakers should price in when assessing reform pledges.
insights.quote: just the tip of the iceberg
insights.locator: The $270bn reported in country submissions to date is

insights.claim: Eva Zabey frames subsidy reform as fiscal policy rather than environmental compliance, arguing 'Subsidy reform should be treated as an economic necessity, not an environmental checklist.'
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reframing harmful-subsidy phase-out as an economic (not just environmental) issue could broaden the political coalition pushing for reform.
insights.quote: Subsidy reform should be treated as an economic necessity, not an environmental checklist.
insights.locator: The positive news is that some countries have shown it can be done

insights.claim: Target 18 of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework requires nations to identify all biodiversity-harmful subsidies by 2025, then eliminate, phase out or reform at least $500bn per year of them by 2030, prioritizing the 'most harmful' incentives first.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The $500bn/year 2030 phase-out target is the concrete policy trigger to watch for fossil fuel, agriculture and fishing subsidy exposure.
insights.locator: Target 18 calls on countries to identify subsidies

insights.claim: A draft UN progress report finds only 38% of countries addressed the 2025 subsidy-identification goal 'to some extent' in their national biodiversity targets, and concludes available evidence suggests the global milestone was not met.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Confirms the miss is systemic and pre-signaled at the UN level, not just an artifact of Carbon Brief's own methodology.
insights.locator: Only 38% of countries addressed the 2025 aim

insights.claim: Harmful subsidies are expected to be a key priority at COP17, the UN nature summit scheduled to be held in Armenia in October 2026.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: COP17 in October 2026 is a concrete near-term catalyst event for new subsidy-reform commitments or pressure on laggard countries.
insights.locator: Harmful subsidies are expected to be among the key priorities

insights.claim: There is no universally agreed definition distinguishing a 'biodiversity-harmful' subsidy from a broader 'environmentally-harmful' subsidy, which undermines consistent measurement across countries' reports.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Definitional ambiguity means cross-country subsidy comparisons (and the $270bn tally itself) should be treated as directional, not precise.
insights.quote: If you were to do a study that focused on biodiversity-harmful subsidies versus one that focused on environmentally-harmful subsidies, there’d be a Venn diagram where a large percentage would overlap.
insights.locator: Paul Elton, a PhD candidate at the Australian National University, tells Carbon Brief

insights.claim: A 2022 OECD working paper treats biodiversity as a narrower subset of the broader 'environment' category, excluding climate and air, even while acknowledging that subsidies causing larger greenhouse gas emissions indirectly harm biodiversity too.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shows that even the reference methodology (OECD) draws boundaries that can undercount climate-linked biodiversity harm, e.g. from fossil-fuel subsidies.
insights.locator: A 2022 working paper on identifying subsidies harmful to biodiversity

insights.claim: Political ecologist Jessica Dempsey (University of British Columbia) says fossil-fuel subsidies should 'absolutely' count as biodiversity-harming, both as climate drivers and via localized extraction damage, arguing subsidies to known drivers of biodiversity loss are an obvious case.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reinforces that fossil-fuel subsidy reform is central to biodiversity policy, not a tangential climate-only issue — relevant for ESG/policy risk screens on fossil-fuel-subsidizing economies.
insights.quote: subsidies to the sectors that are known drivers of biodiversity loss feel very obvious to me.
insights.locator: Prof Jessica Dempsey, a political ecologist at the University of British Columbia, tells Carbon Brief

insights.claim: Global estimates put total biodiversity-harmful subsidies at $1.7-3.2tn per year and total environmentally harmful subsidies at $2.6tn per year, meaning the GBF's $500bn phase-out target covers only roughly a sixth to a third of the estimated total harm.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Even full compliance with the 2030 GBF target would leave the large majority of estimated harmful subsidies untouched, capping the policy's near-term impact.
insights.locator: One recent estimate of the global total of biodiversity-harming subsidies

insights.claim: Paul Elton notes the roughly $250-270bn disclosed so far by reporting countries is only about half of the $500bn phase-out target itself — let alone the multi-trillion-dollar global estimate — calling this 'a significant lack of accountability.'
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the accountability gap: disclosed subsidy figures fall well short even of the phase-out target's own scale, flagging weak enforcement credibility ahead of COP17.
insights.quote: It’s a significant lack of accountability.
insights.locator: It’s useful to contextualise the $500bn ambition of the GBF

insights.claim: Of the subsidies reported to the CBD, almost half are attributed to the fossil-fuel sector and roughly one-quarter to agriculture and fishing combined, per Carbon Brief's standardized categorization of national report data.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Fossil-fuel subsidies remain the single largest disclosed category, making them the priority target for near-term reform and the sector most exposed to phase-out pressure.
insights.locator: Of the subsidies reported to the CBD, almost half were for the fossil-fuel sector

insights.claim: Only one of the 32 countries that provided subsidy data mentioned mining as a sector receiving harmful subsidies, a near-absence that Jessica Dempsey calls 'surprising' given mining's known biodiversity impact.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Mining subsidies appear systematically under-reported relative to their expected biodiversity impact, a data gap worth flagging for anyone assessing mining-sector policy risk.
insights.locator: Dempsey says it is “surprising” that mining “didn’t show up”

insights.claim: Subsidies can have mixed effects — e.g. hydropower dam subsidies harm local biodiversity via disrupted water flows and flooding, but also cut fossil-fuel dependence and emissions — illustrating why, as subsidies expert Ronald Steenblik puts it, 'What's harmful is somewhat in the eye of the beholder.'
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Trade-off subsidies like hydropower complicate simple 'good vs. bad' subsidy classification, meaning country-level 'harmful subsidy' totals depend heavily on methodological line-drawing.
insights.quote: What’s harmful is somewhat in the eye of the beholder.
insights.locator: A subsidy on constructing dams for new hydropower

themes.theme: Data quality gaps and national self-reporting discrepancies

insights.claim: There is no standardized, globally agreed methodology or single global dataset for valuing environmentally or biodiversity-harmful subsidies, per the CBD's own reporting guidance, which undermines comparability of country-reported figures.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The $270bn global tally should be read as a lower-bound, methodology-dependent estimate rather than a precise, comparable figure.
insights.locator: there is no standardised, globally agreed methodology

insights.claim: China's national report claims the country has already identified all of its biodiversity-harming subsidies and reformed them entirely, a claim Carbon Brief presents without independent verification given the absence of a standardized methodology.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Self-reported 'full compliance' claims from major economies like China warrant scrutiny given the lack of standardized verification.
insights.locator: For example, China’s national report says the country has already identified

insights.claim: An independent 2026 study led by Paul Elton found Australia's biodiversity-harmful subsidies totaled $26.3bn over 2022-23 (about 1% of GDP), versus just $155m self-reported in Australia's official national report — roughly a 170x gap.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Illustrates that official government self-reporting can dramatically understate true subsidy exposure; independent academic estimates should be weighted more heavily than national disclosures when assessing country-level biodiversity/fiscal risk.
insights.locator: In Australia, a 2026 study

insights.claim: More than three-quarters of the 134 national reports submitted to the CBD did not list any subsidy figures at all, meaning the $270bn global tally rests on a small minority of highly disclosure-willing countries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The disclosed $270bn figure likely understates true global exposure simply due to non-reporting, reinforcing the 'tip of the iceberg' framing.
insights.locator: More than three-quarters of reports did not list any figures

insights.claim: Jessica Dempsey warns that focusing subsidy reform purely on aggregate dollar totals — without examining who benefits from each subsidy — risks policy changes that worsen affordability for ordinary people and trigger public backlash.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Flags a political/social risk premium on aggressive, blunt subsidy phase-outs (e.g. fuel subsidy cuts), relevant to country-risk and policy-implementation analysis beyond the headline dollar targets.
insights.quote: we really risk having policy changes that then lead to increased affordability problems for everyday working people, and backlash.
